questions.question: What is application-level rate limiting?
options: Waiting for the provider to return a 429 error before doing anything
Imposing a self-set request limit below the provider's actual limit, to avoid unpredictably hitting the hard ceiling
A feature that only exists on the provider's side, not something an application can control
Permanently disabling an AI feature after any single rate limit error
questions.explanation: Application-level rate limiting means deliberately throttling your own request rate below the provider's actual limit, turning an unpredictable failure mode into a predictable, controlled one.

questions.question: Why is prioritization important when a system's AI request capacity is constrained?
options: It ensures all requests are processed in completely random order
It ensures the most important requests (e.g. paying customers, urgent tasks) are processed first when capacity is limited, rather than treating all requests equally under strain
It has no real effect on the user experience during a spike
It is only relevant for background batch jobs, never for user-facing requests
questions.explanation: Combined with a request queue, prioritization ensures that when capacity is constrained, the most important work (e.g. interactive, paying-customer requests) is processed ahead of lower-priority background work.

questions.question: A feature works in testing but fails for many users at once during a real product launch due to hitting a provider's rate limit. Which question best identifies the real gap?
options: Should we just ask the provider to remove rate limits entirely?
Do we throttle ourselves below the provider's actual limit and gracefully degrade under load, or do we only react after hitting a 429 with no queueing or prioritization?
Can we blame the provider and move on without changes?
Should we stop using AI for this feature entirely?
questions.explanation: The real gap is usually the absence of self-imposed throttling, queueing, prioritization, and graceful degradation — the rate limit itself is expected and known; the failure is in how the system responds to reaching it.
